analysis.title: Investment Strategy Weekly Headings (October 30, 2026): Midterm Election Outlook and Weekly Market Review
key_insights: Raymond James' policy team assigns a 90% probability that Democrats flip the House. The Senate is a toss-up, with Democrats needing four seats. Key Senate races are Texas, Michigan, Maine and Alaska.
The 36 gubernatorial races may matter as much as Congress because data center policy is largely set at the state level, which could shape AI policy, investment, growth and equities.

RJ does not expect a blue wave. Democrats lead the Generic House Ballot by 9 points, but few districts are truly competitive, so RJ expects a pickup of about 20 House seats, near the historical average (2010: Republicans +63; 2018: Democrats +44). Early-signal races: VA-02, VA-07, and Iowa and Kentucky districts.

Congress must pass appropriations or a continuing resolution to fund the government beyond December 12 and avoid a shutdown. The debt ceiling is expected to become binding sometime next year. Healthcare and defense spending are the likely negotiation areas.

The president retains broad authority over trade through executive action, so tariffs remain a source of volatility over the next 24 months. Geopolitical and military decisions also rest largely with the president.
RJ ranks politics eighth of 10 fundamental market drivers. Growing data center moratoriums are the exception, because AI is a rising share of investment, growth and earnings.

GDP growth has averaged 2.8% under divided government versus 3.7% under single-party control, and 10 of 13 recessions since 1945 occurred under divided government. RJ keeps its 2027 GDP forecast at 2.3% and is watching for data center delays or moratoriums that slow capex.

S&P 500 returns average about 9.5% annualized under unified government versus 8.2% under divided government. The index has averaged about 15% in the 12 months after a midterm and has been positive after all 21 midterms since 1942. RJ keeps its 12-month S&P 500 target at 8,450.

RJ expects one Fed hike in December over the next 12 months and a 12-month 10-year Treasury yield target of 4.5% to 4.75%, regardless of the election. With the deficit near $2 trillion, RJ expects Treasury auction bid-to-cover around 2.5x.
Betting markets price a 92% chance Democrats take the House and a 67% chance they take the Senate (Polymarket, as of 10/29/2026).
3Q GDP grew 3.4% QoQ annualized, with consumer spending +3.8% and private investment +19.4%, led by equipment.
September headline PCE rose 0.5% MoM and core PCE 0.3% MoM. Year-over-year rates accelerated to 3.6% and 3.1%, and August core PCE was revised higher, pointing to price pressure beyond energy.
Consumer confidence rose to 91.7 in October on easing gasoline prices but remains on a long-term downward trend.

With 61% of S&P 500 market cap reported, consensus 3Q26 EPS growth is 29% y/y, the third straight quarter above 25%. The aggregate EPS beat is only 2%, the weakest since 4Q22, and the S&P 500 is down 1% since earnings season began on 10/13.

Seasonality: since 1950, November and December have been the strongest two-month stretch, averaging more than 3% with positive returns 77% of the time. In midterm years the average is about 4%. RJ stays constructive on US equities into year-end.

The Fed held at 3.75%-4.00% with Cook and Hammack dissenting in favor of a second 25 bp hike. Chair Warsh said September's hike is tightening financial conditions but did not call them restrictive. Intermediate Treasuries rallied on a less hawkish read, and a December hike is about 70% priced.

CCC-rated spreads have nearly doubled since February to 1,096 bps, and the CCC/B spread ratio is about 3.7x, a 99.8th percentile reading since 2000. RJ reads this as stress confined to the weakest borrowers. Spread to B and BB credit would be the larger concern.

The administration warned Gulf partners of a possible short, intense air strike on Iranian leadership, nuclear and energy sites. No final decision has been made. VP Vance opened a channel with Iranian security officials. The US wants nuclear concessions first, while Tehran wants relief from the naval blockade and sanctions first.
German consumer sentiment (GfK) has been negative for 60 consecutive months, a headwind for euro zone growth.

Lula's unexpected reelection drove Brazil's Bovespa to its steepest one-day drop since 2020 and the real to its sharpest drop since 1999. RJ views the selloff as excessive because Brazil's fundamentals follow commodity prices more than policy.

Week ahead: JOLTS Tuesday, expected firmly above 7 million for a sixth month. AMD earnings Tuesday evening for AI capex read-through after slightly soft hyperscaler capex. Treasury quarterly refunding starts Monday afternoon. The October jobs report is Friday, with RJ expecting +70,000 versus an unrevised +29,000 in September.

sector_views.rationale: RJ is constructive on US equities into year-end and beyond, citing resilient earnings, AI capex, and post-midterm seasonality.

Hyperscaler capex reported this week was slightly softer than expected (reported). AMD reports Tuesday evening (upcoming, 11/3) and is the next read on AI infrastructure spending.

The Russia/Ukraine war continues to weigh on European consumer confidence, especially in Germany.

tension_points.bull_case: S&P 500 has gained about 15% on average in the 12 months after a midterm and been positive after all 21 since 1942. November and December are seasonally strong, and earnings are resilient.
tension_points.bear_case: Returns and GDP growth have historically been weaker under divided government, and 10 of 13 recessions since 1945 occurred under it. Data center moratoriums could slow AI capex, and the weakest EPS beat rate since 4Q22 has the index down 1% in earnings season.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Data center delays or moratoriums that slow capex momentum and create downside risk to the 2.3% 2027 GDP forecast.

theme_stances.key_argument: The S&P 500 has historically gained after midterms regardless of the winner, and with strong earnings that supports the 8,450 target.
CCC widening alone has not reliably signaled significant trouble for the S&P 500, so spread to B and BB would be the bigger concern.
theme_stances.evidence: stress among the weakest borrowers rather than broad deterioration
